card.hook: Picture a huge white castle sitting on top of a hill like a cake on a stand. That's Hohensalzburg, and the hill does half the posing for you.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 540 m south of the fortress, and face north. That's far enough to fit the whole fortress and the hillside below it in one shot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for one wide shot that shows the whole hill. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the towers and the line of the walls. Skip 0.5x here, because it makes the fortress look tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the line of the walls on the upper third line, and tap the walls so they stay sharp and bright, then slide a touch darker if the sky is glaring.
card.best_time: Late morning to afternoon is likely to be your best bet, because the sun should be behind you and shining on the south-facing walls. If it's overcast, the walls look flatter, so zoom in on the towers for more interest.
card.selfie_here: Head to the middle of the Makartsteg (also called Marko-Feingold-Steg), the pedestrian bridge over the Salzach, and face up the river. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x to squeeze in the fortress above the Old Town spires, with the padlock-covered railings giving you a fun foreground.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Rose Hill lookout in Mirabell Gardens while you stand in the foreground park, so the fortress is behind you and Mirabell Palace sits off to one side.
card.rules_and_safety: The fortress itself may be ticketed or have restricted areas, so check the official site before you go. Rose Hill is very popular, so it's best to arrive early.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole hill, then one close-up where you can count the towers along the ridge. Bonus points if the horizon stays dead level!
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1077, and the prince-archbishops kept adding to it for centuries. It's about 250 m long and 150 m wide, which makes it one of the largest medieval castles in Europe, and it was never taken by force. It also has the Reisszug, an early funicular first described in 1515 and probably the oldest working railway in the world.

card.hook: Picture clipped boxwood in neat swirls, mythological statues on every corner and a pale palace closing the view at the far end. Mirabell is a garden that looks like it was planned for your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 180 m south of the subject, and face north towards the palace. Let the garden paths lead your eye straight up to it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the palace with the garden in front of it. Go to 0.5x when you want the whole garden pattern in the frame. Use 2x or more for statues, fountain details and the palace front without people in the foreground.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the palace on the upper line, and let a path or flowerbed edge run in from the bottom of the frame.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually the quietest time, and the light is softer. Later the gardens get busier, so be ready to wait for a gap between visitors.
card.selfie_here: Walk into the middle of the Grand Parterre lawn, a few steps down from the palace side, and turn your back to the palace. A travel guide calls this one of the most iconic photos in the gardens. For a Sound of Music pose, try the wide stone steps beside the Pegasus fountain (the Do-Re-Mi steps). Use the front camera at 0.5x if you want more of the scene behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the formal garden in front of the palace's garden façade, with the windows and roofline behind them, while you step back along the path to frame it.
card.rules_and_safety: The gardens are a public attraction, but check the official site before you go for current access rules. The palace is a working city hall, and its interior is mostly closed to tourists.
card.challenge: Get a shot where the path leads to the palace and nobody is in the gap, then hum Do-Re-Mi for your reward.
card.good_to_know: The palace dates from about 1606, when Prince-Archbishop Wolf Dietrich built it as a pleasure palace. It was rebuilt in Baroque style in the 1720s and got its present Neoclassical look around 1818, after a fire. Today it houses the mayor's office and city departments, and the Marble Hall is used for concerts and weddings.

card.hook: Picture a tall yellow house squeezed into a busy shopping lane, with shopfronts at its feet and people drifting past like it's any old Tuesday. That's where Mozart was born, and the whole scene fits in one photo.
card.stand_here: On Getreidegasse, stand about 140 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Take a wider shot there that shows the street leading to the house, then walk east for about 2 minutes to No. 9 for close-ups.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the main shot, and switch to 0.5x if the lane is too narrow to fit the whole front of the house. Try zoom 2x or more (depends on your phone) for the doorway, so you don't have to stand in the way.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep your phone upright so the walls stand straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning or late evening usually means fewer people in the lane, so it's easier to get a clear shot of the house.
card.selfie_here: Try the shop windows on Getreidegasse opposite the yellow house at No. 9 and play with the reflections, which can put the house behind you in the frame. Use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the house over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Hagenauerplatz at the Getreidegasse corner, where the marker is, while you stand in front of the yellow No. 9 front.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are usually not allowed inside the museum, and flash is prohibited, so check the signs when you go in. The floors are uneven, so wear comfy shoes.
card.challenge: Find the tiny coiled serpent in a lion's mouth over the doorway and get a close-up before anyone walks into your shot.
card.good_to_know: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born here on 27 January 1756. His family rented the third-floor flat from 1747 to 1773. The house has been a museum since 1880, and it's also called the Hagenauerhaus, after the family who owned it from 1703. Right next to it: Getreidegasse.

card.hook: Picture a pale pink-and-cream palace sitting right on the edge of a lake, with lawns and trees around it. Schloss Leopoldskron looks like a postcard before you've even lifted your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 230 m west of Schloss Leopoldskron, and face east. From there the whole 74 m-wide palace fits in your photo easily.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the palace, the lake and the trees in one go. Then tap 2x to tighten up on the façade and leave out the clutter. Zoom 0.5x gives you lots of sky and water, but the palace shrinks to a toy.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the palace on one of the vertical lines and let the water fill the bottom third of the frame.
card.best_time: In the afternoon the sun is behind you as you look east, so it lights up the side of the palace facing you. On a calm early morning the lake may give you a reflection too.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the public footpath on the south or west shore of the Leopoldskroner Weiher and turn your back to the water. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and let the palace sit over your shoulder. On a still day its reflection comes along for the photo.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo from a few steps back along the path while you stand by the small public bench under the shade trees on the western shore, which lines up with the palace façade.
card.rules_and_safety: The palace is a private hotel, so stay out of the private grounds and follow any signs. Swimming in summer and ice-skating in winter aren't allowed on the lake, so keep to walking and photos.
card.challenge: Can you get the palace, a leafy branch and its wobbly reflection into one frame without anyone photobombing?
card.good_to_know: Prince-Archbishop Leopold Anton von Firmian had the palace built in 1736 beside an existing pond. In 1918 the theatre director Max Reinhardt, co-founder of the Salzburg Festival, bought it and spent about twenty years restoring it. Film fans, note that the palace itself never appears in The Sound of Music. Some scenes were shot on the neighbouring Meierhof grounds, using replicas of the palace's terrace and gate.

card.hook: The cathedral's front is bright marble, but the rest of the church is dark grey stone, so the pale façade pops like a spotlight. It's also far too big to squeeze in from close up, so pick your shot before you raise your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 40 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east towards the façade. For the column-and-façade shot, walk back to the centre of the arcades at the back of Domplatz.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the façade, both towers and some of the square. Switch to 1x for a more natural look at the front. Then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the saints' statues, the gable and the golden crown.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the marble façade, then slide the brightness down a touch so the pale stone keeps its detail and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the day or later in the afternoon, when the square is usually quieter and the light on the marble is softer. Check how the light hits the front when you arrive, and shuffle a few steps if there's glare.
card.selfie_here: Try Kapitelplatz beside the Sphaera sculpture, the golden globe with a figure on top, so the cathedral's south façade is behind you. Another option is the Residenzbrunnen fountain on Residenzplatz with the cathedral in the background. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold the phone a little low so the cathedral sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Kapitelschwemme well on Kapitelplatz and frame you with the cathedral's south side behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is open to walk through, but the cathedral is a working place of worship, so dress respectfully and check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.
card.challenge: Walk back to the centre of the arcades and line up the Maria Immaculata column so the golden crown seems to float right above the figure.
card.good_to_know: The present cathedral was consecrated in 1628 and replaced an older church that was badly damaged in 1598. It's 142 metres long and 33 metres high at the crossing. Mozart was baptised here in 1756, and the Maria Immaculata column in Domplatz went up between 1766 and 1771.

card.hook: Getreidegasse looks like a lane that's slowly closing in on you, with tall houses elbowing each other and iron guild signs dangling over every shopfront. It's one of Salzburg's busiest streets, so grab the calm view of it from above first.
card.stand_here: Stand about 330 m west of the subject, on Museum der Moderne (the phone icon on the map), and face east. You'll look east and down over the roofs onto the Getreidegasse, with the Festival Hall and the Salzach beyond.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the wide view with the Festival Hall and the river. Then try zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the rooftops and the line of the street. Down in the lane, zoom 0.5x squeezes in those tall facades.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the street along a lower grid line and keep the horizon level, then tap the roofs and slide it a bit darker if the sky is bright so the roofs keep their colour.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning if you want the street with few people, because it's crowded from late morning on. The terrace is quieter, but check the lift times before you head up.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the bright yellow facade of Mozart's Birthplace at No. 9, with the building right behind you. Use the front camera and tilt it up a little so the yellow fills the background. For a change from the open street, try the arcade passage that links Getreidegasse to University Square, where the layered shop canopies and green flower boxes make a ready-made backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement across the street from No. 9 while you pose in front of the yellow facade, with the shop windows opposite as the setting.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos for personal use are fine on public streets like this one, but be mindful of private businesses and their entrances. The lift up to the terrace may have its own rules or hours, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Find a guild sign you love, then catch it with the narrow lane running away behind it, and wait for a gap with no people walking through.
card.good_to_know: The street is mentioned as far back as about 1150, under a different name, and it was a trading street long before it was a shopping one. Mozart was born at No. 9 and the family lived there until 1773. The building has housed a Mozart museum since 1880. Many houses hide passageways and courtyards, so look for gaps between the shops.

card.hook: Up on the old city-wall platform, Nonnberg Abbey looks small, tucked below the fortress across a sea of rooftops. That's the charm: you're not shooting one building, you're shooting a whole town with a convent in it.
card.stand_here: Head to the old city-wall platform on Kapuzinerberg, near the Kapuzinerkloster, about 510 m north of the abbey. Face south and look across the city.
card.zoom: At zoom 1x the abbey will look tiny, so try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick it out. Keep a little rooftop and sky in the frame so it still feels like Salzburg.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the abbey on a crossing point, then tap it and slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and clearer detail on the walls.
card.selfie_here: Try the small lookout terrace right in front of the abbey's entrance gate: use the front camera, zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the gate over your shoulder. The stone Nonnbergstiege steps are another option, where you can catch the convent above you.
card.ask_someone: On the Kapuzinerberg platform, ask someone to stand a few steps back facing south while you stand by the wall, so the rooftops and the abbey sit behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The abbey is reached by steep steps and cobblestone paths, not by car, so wear comfy shoes. Inside, only the church and cemetery are open to visitors.
card.challenge: Spot the Kajetanerkirche dome and try to keep it just inside the left edge while the abbey sits on a gridline crossing.
card.good_to_know: Nonnberg Abbey is a Benedictine convent founded around 712/715 by Saint Rupert. It's described as the oldest continuously existing nunnery in the German-speaking world. It's part of Salzburg's UNESCO-listed historic centre, and Maria von Trapp's story, which became The Sound of Music, began here.

card.hook: Here's a nice surprise: you don't need a long walk or fiddly settings at Alter Markt. The café frontage, the buildings and the open square all squeeze into one phone shot.
card.stand_here: Head to Alter Markt, where Café Tomaselli sits, and stand at the phone icon on the map, about 35 m south-east of the café. Face north-west and the café is about 34 m ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the square and café together. Go to 0.5x if you want more of the buildings, but keep the café away from the very edges so it doesn't look stretched. Then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the signs and café windows.

card.challenge: Take one wide shot with the café on one side and open square on the other, then a close-up of the café's sign, and see if they look like they belong in the same story.
card.good_to_know: Alter Markt is a square in Salzburg, and Café Tomaselli sits right on it. card.hook: You've puffed up a wooded ridge, and then the whole old town opens out below you: rooftops, church towers and mountains stacked up behind. It's the sort of view that makes you say "oh!" out loud.
card.stand_here: Stand about 770 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, up on the Mönchsberg, and face east toward the old town.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole view in. Try 0.5x if you want a wall or some trees in the foreground, then zoom 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out church towers and rooftops.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines to keep the skyline level, then tap the old town and nudge the slider a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, nicer light. In the evening, try night mode on the lit-up old town and rest your arms against a wall to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the Humboldt Terrace (Humboldtterrasse): it's a small terrace with an open panorama of the Old Town, so the view sits right behind you. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold the phone a little high so the rooftops fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On the terrace in front of the Museum der Moderne, next to the lift entrance, ask a passer-by to frame you with the Old Town behind you and Festung Hohensalzburg in the upper right of the view.
card.rules_and_safety: In rain, the paths can get damp and slick, so take care. The lift and the museum terrace may be ticketed or have set hours, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one zoomed shot from the same spot, then see if you can find the Untersberg in the distance.
card.good_to_know: The Mönchsberg rises to 508 metres and is part of Salzburg's UNESCO World Heritage Site. A lift inside the mountain has served the top since 1890. In 1669 a rockfall onto the streets below caused great loss of life, and a mountain inspector has checked the rock face ever since.

card.hook: Salzburg's old town has a big green curtain hanging behind it, and this is the spot where you see the whole thing. The hill is wooded, and it's dotted with walls, bastions and little towers, so there's plenty to look at.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 550 m south-west of Kapuzinerberg, and face north-east. From there the wooded slope rises up and fills your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole wooded slope in. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the walls, towers and cloister buildings. Save 0.5x for when you're up among the paths and walls, where space is tight.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the tree line along the top third, then tap the hillside and slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is bright, so the greens keep their detail.
card.best_time: Afternoon or early evening usually gives soft, warm light on the slope. On a grey, overcast day the greens look even and rich, so it's still worth going.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the stone terrace of the Hettwer Bastei and stand by the low walls and benches with the Salzach and Old Town behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the view, and keep the Old Town and Hohensalzburg Fortress over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Wear shoes with a decent grip, because these are hillside paths. Check the official site before you go for the cloister, the restaurant at the Franziskischlössl and any seasonal path closures.
card.challenge: Climb up and find a gap in the trees that frames the Altstadt like a picture frame, then take your shot through it.
card.good_to_know: Kapuzinerberg is 640 metres high and part of Salzburg's UNESCO World Heritage Site. A Capuchin cloister was built here between 1599 and 1605, on the site of a medieval fortress. The walls and bastions date from 1629, in the time of the Thirty Years' War, and the path up from Linzergasse passes 13 oratories with the Way of the Cross, built between 1736 and 1744.

card.hook: Three postcards for the price of one: iron crosses up close, an abbey church in the middle, and Hohensalzburg Fortress perched on the cliff behind. And it's usually quieter here than in the old town streets.
card.stand_here: Stand at Petersfriedhof (the phone icon on the map), about 65 m south-east of the subject, and face north-west. The graves fill the bottom of your shot, the abbey church sits in the middle, and the fortress rises behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to grab the whole scene, then try 1x for a calmer, more natural look. If your phone has zoom 2x to 5x, use it to pick out the church tower, the fortress or the chapel details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the church, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stonework doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, according to one guide, when the light is softer. Check the shady spots under the trees and arcades too, as they can look darker than the sky.
card.selfie_here: Walk the flagstone paths between the flowered graves and turn so the rock face and arcades are behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold the phone a bit lower, so the cliff and arcades fill the frame over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand in the main courtyard in front of the hexagonal marble fountain and ask your helper to back off far enough to fit the whole church facade behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The cemetery is a working burial ground, so photograph quietly, keep your distance from mourners, and don't photograph people or private memorials without permission. Photos inside the church may be restricted, so check before you shoot. One older visitor account says the catacomb windows are barred with a dangerous cliff drop beyond, so stay behind the barriers.
card.challenge: Get crosses along the bottom edge, the church in the middle and the fortress at the top, all in one frame, without a single stranger's face.
card.good_to_know: St Peter's Abbey was founded in 696 by Saint Rupert and is described as the oldest monastery in the German-speaking area with a continuous history since its foundation. The Romanesque church went up from about 1130 and was dedicated in 1147, and the onion-domed steeple dates from 1756. The oldest surviving graves in the cemetery date from 1288 and 1300.

card.hook: Your Salzburg album is probably full of street-level close-ups, so this is the stop that gives it a big scene-setter. There are benches up here too, which your feet will appreciate.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 15 m north-east of the subject at Richterhöhe, and face south-west. Take a second to look around first and pick a clear line of sight.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view. Tap 0.5x to squeeze in more of the scene, or try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out far-off details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom line if you can see it, and keep your main subject across the middle.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, more flattering light than midday. Check the weather first, because a clear day makes the biggest difference.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Richterhöhe lookout platform, beside the Eduard-Richter monument and the benches. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the monument in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: If you're down at the Leopoldskroner Weiher, stand on the shore in front of Schloss Leopoldskron and ask someone to take your photo facing up toward Richterhöhe, with the fortress visible beyond it.
card.rules_and_safety: In winter, paths may be icy or snowy, so wear shoes with good grip. Watch your footing while you line up the shot, and check the official site before you go in case of access restrictions.

card.best_time: Soft, overcast light is your friend here. It keeps colours even and avoids harsh shadows, so a grey day is a good day.

card.hook: Here's a secret: a river and a bridge are the easiest photo partners going. The Salzach gives you wide open space, the Staatsbrücke gives you bold lines, and the buildings along the banks fill in the background.
card.stand_here: Head for the Salzach river at the Staatsbrücke in Salzburg and stand about 15 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south, look along the water and let the bridge sit across your picture.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the river and bridge. Go 0.5x if you want more bank and sky, or 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out details of the bridge.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the bridge up with one of the horizontal lines so it doesn't look tilted.
card.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset gives softer light, and the lights after dusk can add reflections on the water. Midday sun may be behind the bridge when you face south, so check your screen for glare.
card.selfie_here: Stop at the railing about halfway across the Staatsbrücke, where you get river views both ways. Or try the riverbank at the Old Town end, where Getreidegasse meets the Salzach. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the bridge and water over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Makartsteg footbridge, just north of the Staatsbrücke, and aim back at the bridge while you pose on it.
card.rules_and_safety: The Staatsbrücke is a busy junction with cars and trolleybuses, so use the pedestrian crossings to get across the road. On a busy pavement, keep your phone close to your body so you don't block anyone.
card.challenge: Take a few frames as cyclists, boats or people pass, then pick the one with the cleanest gaps and a perfectly level bridge.
card.good_to_know: This is an open public riverside spot, but check the official site before you go in case of local restrictions. The Makartsteg is the footbridge just north of the Staatsbrücke. Getreidegasse ends at the Salzach near the bridge on the Old Town side.

card.hook: Water in front, stone in the middle, church towers at the back: Residenzplatz stacks its photo in neat layers, and you get all of them in one go. Just keep an eye out for a stage or a market stall wandering into your shot.
card.stand_here: Stand about 40 m east of the subject, at Residenzbrunnen (the phone icon on the map), and face west. The fountain is to the west of you, with Salzburg Cathedral rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the whole fountain and the cathedral squeeze into one picture. Want a calmer view of just the fountain? Switch to zoom 1x and step back a little.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the fountain on your screen, then drag the brightness down a touch if the sky looks washed out, so the stone and the cathedral stay clear.
card.best_time: Go before 9:00 or after 20:00 and you'll dodge most of the crowds. In summer, the golden light is roughly 18:30-20:00.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and turn so the big landmark sits over your shoulder. Hold the phone a bit higher and a little away from you to fit more in.

card.rules_and_safety: Street performers, horse carriages, the Christmas market and temporary stages can crowd or block the fountain, so check the square on the day.
card.challenge: Can you get all three layers in one frame: the fountain, the cathedral and the Residenz buildings at the sides, with no one's head in the way?
card.good_to_know: Residenzplatz is a wide paved square with a Baroque fountain, and the Residenz buildings frame it from the sides. It's open at all hours, but events and markets can change what you see. In winter the fountain is sometimes boarded up, so you might not see any water.

card.hook: A big golden ball sitting out in an open square is hard to walk past, and your phone is going to want a picture of it. The good news is the buildings around Kapitelplatz make a handsome backdrop.
card.stand_here: Stand in Kapitelplatz about 50 m north-west of the Sphaera, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Then walk a few steps left or right until the buildings sit neatly around the sculpture.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the sculpture with its surroundings. Try 0.5x if you want more of the buildings and space, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a closer look at the sculpture itself.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put the sculpture on one of the vertical lines instead of dead centre, then tap it and nudge the slider darker if any bright patches look washed out.
card.best_time: Pick a moment when the sun isn't directly behind the sculpture. A lightly clouded sky softens the glare on shiny surfaces, while a clear sky gives a bright, clean look. Crowds tend to peak around midday, so wait a moment for a gap if it's busy.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the open paving in Kapitelplatz right in front of the Sphaera, with the sphere behind you and the Cathedral in the frame. Use the front camera at 0.5x if you can, and for a classic shot, move around a few steps until Hohensalzburg Fortress lines up directly behind the sphere.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand where Domplatz opens into Kapitelplatz, facing the sphere, while you stand in front of it so the Cathedral and sphere both fit in the shot.
card.challenge: Take one shot from far back, then crouch low and tilt up so the top of the sphere sits against the sky. Which one would you frame?
card.good_to_know: The Sphaera is a sculpture in Kapitelplatz, Salzburg. If you move a step or two to either side, you may spot small details in its curved surface. We don't have dates or measurements for it, so look for a plaque or sign beside it if you want the details.

selfie_spots.why: Guides say the sculpture is prominently displayed in the square and that the Cathedral can be seen in the same frame, so a selfie there keeps the landmark in view.

card.hook: From the phone icon, the Kollegienkirche plays hard to get. It's about 188 m away, so at 1x it looks pretty small. Don't worry, a quick zoom fixes that.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 190 m south of the Kollegienkirche, and face north. The church is straight ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole scene, then tap 2x to fill the frame with the building. Want rooftops, people and sky? Try 0.5x, but keep the church in the middle so its edges don't stretch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the church's vertical edges with them so the building stands up straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday, when the sky can look flat and bright. Check which way the front of the church faces that day, because it might be in shade.
card.selfie_here: Try the Furtwänglerpark, the green strip beside the church, and see if you can get the building behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and tilt the phone until the church shows over your shoulder. I can't promise the angle works there, so have a play.
card.ask_someone: Herbert-von-Karajan-Platz is a square with the church in view, so try standing there and asking a passer-by to take a full-facade shot of you with the church behind.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship, so it may have set visiting times or rules. Check the official site before you go in, including anything about photography.
card.challenge: Take the same shot at 0.5x, 1x and 2x, then pick your favourite. Bonus points if you dodge every lamp post and sign.
card.good_to_know: The Collegiate Church (Kollegienkirche) is a church in Salzburg and one of the stops on this map. It's a place of worship, so visiting arrangements can apply. From the phone icon it's about 188 m, or roughly 3 minutes on foot.

card.hook: Don't go hunting for one favourite building on Linzer Gasse. The star here is the whole street, with the rows on either side pulling your eye down the road like a pair of arrows.
card.stand_here: Stand about 100 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. That gives you the street opening up in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x with gridlines on, and keep the phone level. If the street feels cramped, tap 0.5x. If your phone has zoom 2x, use it for a tighter, more layered view.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the sky, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually kinder to the building fronts than harsh midday sun. Check the light on the day and make it brighter or darker to suit.
card.selfie_here: Try the fountain in front of the arched gate at Linzer Gasse 14, where the stairway up the Kapuzinerberg starts. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the gate over your shoulder. Or try the Platzl, where Linzer Gasse begins.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Stefan-Zweig-Platz corner by the Gablerbräu sign, facing east along the street, while you stand in the street with the houses receding behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The climb up the Kapuzinerberg from Linzer Gasse is steep with lots of stairs, so save your energy for it. It's an ordinary public street, but check local signs on the day for any restrictions.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd, then catch three people walking in the middle distance so the street looks properly lived in.
card.good_to_know: Linzer Gasse is a street in the city of Salzburg. No train stations or tram stops are listed for this spot, so plan to reach it on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

card.hook: A railing covered in padlocks, a fortress perched on a cliff, and a river sliding underneath. Salzburg's footbridge gets a lot into one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand about 80 m north of the subject, on Elisabethkai (the phone icon on the map), and face south. The footbridge fills the foreground, with the Old Town roofs and Hohensalzburg Fortress behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the bridge, the roofs and the fortress in one go. If the bridge gets cut off, drop to 0.5x. For a tighter shot of the fortress above the roofs, try 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the bridge along the lower third and keep the horizon level, so the fortress has room above the roofs.
card.best_time: Soft morning or evening light is usually kinder to the roofs and the fortress. Take a few frames, because people walking across the bridge will wander in and out of your shot.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the middle of the Makartsteg (Marko-Feingold-Steg). Use the front camera, hold it a little low and wide (0.5x if your phone has it), and let the lock-covered railing and the fortress frame you from behind.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand along Elisabethkai, where the bridge sits in the foreground with the fortress behind it, while you pose on the bridge.
card.rules_and_safety: Hold your phone tightly and keep your belongings secure, because the bridge railing has wide gaps.
card.challenge: Catch someone walking across the bridge with the fortress sitting just above the roofs behind them. Bonus points if they have no idea they're in your photo.
card.good_to_know: This footbridge over the Salzach is known for the padlocks on its railings. Its official name is Marko-Feingold-Steg, after it was renamed in 2021 from Makartsteg, and both names are used locally and on maps. The padlocks are removed from time to time when the railings get too heavy, so the locks you see may differ from older photos.

card.hook: Picture a calm river, a cyclist rolling past, and the water's edge pointing you into the scene like a big arrow. That's the Giselakai, and it's a lovely place for an easy, no-stress photo.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon on the map, about 470 m north-west of the subject, and face south-east at the Giselakai riverside view. The subject is far from here, so zoom in rather than walking towards traffic.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole riverside scene in. Then tap 2x to pull the far bank closer, and use 0.5x only if you're right by the water and want lots of sky and water.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and run the water's edge along a lower line so it leads the eye down the river.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer people. It's also a favourite sunset stretch. On grey days the water can look flat, so include more of the surroundings.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the Giselakai riverside promenade, where you can see the Hohensalzburg Fortress. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and tilt the phone so the fortress sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: If you're near the Mozartsteg footbridge, ask someone standing in the middle of it to take your photo while you stand on the Giselakai promenade.
card.rules_and_safety: Cyclists and traffic use the riverside, so keep an eye out and wait for a gap. It looks like an open public area, but check local signs.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one closer shot from the same spot, then see if you can catch a frame with no cyclists in it.
card.good_to_know: The Giselakai is a riverside view on the Salzburg map. On calm days the water can give you mirror-like reflections. Passers-by, cyclists and traffic come and go, so a little patience pays off.
